Citing a METR trial in which experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with AI tools despite estimating they had been 20% faster, Mohanty warns that buying more tool seats only lengthens the review queue. The proposed fix is to plan verification capacity alongside delivery estimates, scale review effort to what breaks if a change is wrong, make sure each merged change's named owner can explain it, and deliberately put junior engineers on verification work.


Sources:

  • How Much Of Last Quarter’s Code Can Your Team Explain? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Soumendra Mohanty

item.title: When To Build Your Own AI Model (And When To Stop Kidding Yourself)
item.description:
Reshef, cofounder of Gong, says post-training a small model can beat off-the-shelf options on a narrow task, but dismisses startup claims that fine-tuning creates a "proprietary moat" because real defensibility comes from proprietary data, feedback loops, strong evals and the harness around the model. Reshef's test weighs scale (millions of inference calls a month, not thousands), how narrow and repeatable the task is, whether prompting has been pushed as far as it can go, and whether simply renegotiating an API contract would do the job. Fine-tuned models also need hosting and periodic retraining as they age, so Reshef advises starting broad and specializing only "when the task is stable and the economics justify it."


Sources:

  • When To Build Your Own AI Model (And When To Stop Kidding Yourself) - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Eilon Reshef

item.title: Why Most Enterprise AI Spending Automates The Wrong Part
item.description:
When Superlinked had to rebuild its outbound sales with fewer people, Gutkovich first had Claude write more emails to more people, which raised volume while replies "barely moved." Noting that 56% of CEOs in PwC's 2026 survey reported no significant financial benefit from AI, Gutkovich argues most spending speeds up single tasks while the bottleneck just moves, and describes redesigning around the outcome instead: agents now watch GitHub issues for engineers describing problems Superlinked solves and tailor outreach to them, while a person signs off on any first message to a senior leader. An early version contacted the projects' own maintainers, often competitors, a misfire Gutkovich found more instructive than weeks of trouble-free operation.


Sources:

  • Why Most Enterprise AI Spending Automates The Wrong Part - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Ben Gutkovich

item.title: As AI Videos Terrify Hollywood, Is It Time To Hand IP Management To The Masses?
item.description:
Citing a viral Seedance 2.0 rooftop fight between AI versions of Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise, made from a two-line prompt, and Disney's cease-and-desist letter to ByteDance, McKenna argues that studios cannot scale enforcement fast enough to contain AI-generated use of their characters. McKenna, cofounder of Alien Worlds, proposes handing IP stewardship to fan communities on the model of Bitcoin's consensus rules, with on-chain voting and built-in arbitration deciding what counts as official canon. McKenna concedes the idea does little about people who monetize famous characters with AI, acknowledging "There are no easy answers."


Sources:

  • As AI Videos Terrify Hollywood, Is It Time To Hand IP Management To The Masses? - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Saro McKenna

item.title: Enterprise Software No Longer Has Just One User
item.description:
Bose, Asana's chief product officer, argues that AI agents won't kill the enterprise user interface but add a second kind of participant, one that needs structured, machine-readable context on ownership, permissions, approvals and past decisions to work safely. People still direct, inspect and judge the work, Bose writes, citing Asana research in which 85% of surveyed workers said a person should review everything agents produce, and predicting chat will serve as "an entry point rather than the whole product." The larger task is a shared "company brain" so humans and agents work from the same organizational context, the gap 73% of IT decision makers in earlier Asana research blamed for AI initiatives at least sometimes failing or stalling.


Sources:

  • Enterprise Software No Longer Has Just One User - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Arnab Bose

item.title: Can Your Callers Reach You? A Regulator Will Want The Evidence That Says So
item.description:
Dunne, CEO of call-testing company Klearcom, argues that when regulators examine voice channels, the question is whether callers can reach a company and whether it can prove it, yet in Dunne's experience many contact center leaders cannot say who owns the line from the carrier to the end of the call. Klearcom's test calls keep turning up gaps: roughly one in 10 lines at a U.S. health insurer failed to connect or played a leftover test recording, and nearly 15% of calls to a life sciences customer's lines in China failed, clustered around the emergency option for serious reactions. Dunne recommends a single accountable owner, a higher standard for regulated lines such as adverse-event and card-blocking numbers, testing from outside the company's own systems like a real caller, and retesting whenever routing, menus, platforms or AI models change.


Sources:

  • Can Your Callers Reach You? A Regulator Will Want The Evidence That Says So - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Liam Dunne

item.title: 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow
item.description:
Forbes Technology Council members name startup habits that established tech companies should keep as process and hierarchy pile up. Vytautas Savickas of Oxylabs urges firms to keep turning down business that doesn't fit, Rob Sloan of Zscaler wants authority pushed to "the people closest to the problem" and Akhilesh Sharma of A3Logics argues every new priority should displace an old one. Sergii Grushai of Peeklogic recommends running a process by hand before automating it, noting that "roughly a third of flows" in the mature organizations Peeklogic audits either duplicate another or barely run.


Sources:

  • 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Expert Panel, Forbes Technology Council

item.title: Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses
item.description:
Mudavatu uses EchoLeak, a since-patched Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw disclosed in June 2025 that let a crafted email trigger data exfiltration without a click, to argue that enterprise AI security now depends on "enforceable boundaries" more than on reassuring model behavior. The proposed framework assesses six blind spots, including unverified model artifacts, agents whose credentials outlive being disabled, data leaking through tool calls and logs, and trust inherited between agents, then phases in controls starting with agent discovery, outbound monitoring and kill switches. Mudavatu would count a control as closed only with evidence that it works, and offers a simple test: disable an agent and confirm its downstream actions actually stop.


Sources:

  • Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Vasanth Mudavatu

item.title: Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies
item.description:
Goel, CEO of Cyware, argues that threat intelligence feeds know the threat but nothing about a subscriber's own assets, identities and controls, so relevance has to be produced by measuring each indicator against a specific environment. The same indicator can call for immediate isolation at a company where it maps to a critical internet-facing application and mere logging where it touches a decommissioned service; without that context, Goel writes, an indicator "is just a rumor about someone else's network." That matters more as platforms and AI agents rather than human analysts consume intelligence to prioritize and act, since raw one-size-fits-all feeds leave them unable to tell a live risk from an irrelevant one.


Sources:

  • Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Anuj Goel

item.title: The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way
item.description:
Kaluvuri, CEO of ApyHub, points to a large bank that gives an AI agent a name, a login ID and a manager, and argues that approval workflows can't oversee software taking thousands of autonomous actions because "the risk lives in the path." Finance learned this through episodes like Knight Capital's loss of more than $460 million in 45 minutes in 2012 and moved controls into the execution path, with the SEC's market access rule requiring them to stay under a firm's "direct and exclusive control." Kaluvuri urges buyers of agent platforms to ask where runtime controls are enforced and who can change them, and in some cases to keep a workflow under human supervision until adequate controls exist.


Sources:

  • The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Samuel Kaluvuri

item.title: Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes
item.description:
Kolandaisami, a doctoral researcher, recounts an organization that bought an AI coding assistant without studying where it would help and then set a KPI that developers met simply by showing they had adopted the tool. Citing one 2025 study that estimated a 26.08% gain in completed tasks and another that found experienced open-source developers took 19% longer with the AI tools tested, Kolandaisami argues that results vary by environment and that metrics should come from the problem, such as the full cycle from requirements to release rather than programming time alone. Low usage should first be treated as information rather than a performance problem, and pilots should test whether a tool fits a team's people and processes, because "Technology needs to work for us."


Sources:

  • Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Gayathri Kolandaisami

item.title: Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows
item.description:
Ercanbrack, CTO at Vasion, argues that AI governance is usually scoped to the application while documents keep moving through printing, faxing, exporting and scanning, a gap long covered by employees who could remember what they produced. Agents remove that undocumented human control just as adoption accelerates: Deloitte's 2026 survey found nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Ercanbrack suggests following one operational document from creation to disposition and testing identity, authorization, audit and retention at each handoff, since "The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it."


Sources:

  • Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Corey Ercanbrack

item.title: The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure
item.description:
Wong, an AI research fellow at Info-Tech Research Group, sorts national AI energy strategies into four types: sovereign regulation-driven (Canada, Australia, the EU), market-driven (the U.S. and UK), localization-driven (Japan, and South Korea, which is directing 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul) and state-driven China. Wong proposes judging a strategy along its energy value chain, from power sourcing and grid management, where AI racks demanding 130 to 600 kW push operators toward ±400V or 800V DC systems, to thermal management, where some cold-climate operators sell 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat to district heating networks. Builders should also be ready to answer community backlash over data centers with a focus on sustainability, environmental impact and accountability.


Sources:

  • The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Bill Wong

item.title: If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation
item.description:
Bise, CTO of Inbenta, says the knowledge underneath a customer-experience AI deployment, not the model, explains nearly every underperforming one Bise has examined, so buying a new platform is often "an expensive way to rebuild the same problem." Before another vendor evaluation, Bise suggests checking whether content is structured for a model to parse, counting duplicate knowledge stores left from older intent-matching systems or split by channel, and confirming that subject matter experts can fix wrong answers without filing an engineering ticket. AI can now structure and tag content in weeks rather than quarters, and fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of a six-figure platform replacement while producing an audit trail regulators can follow.


Sources:

  • If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Merlin Bise

item.title: Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed
item.description:
Garg, CEO of One Identity, argues that companies don't need new governance architectures for AI agents, because existing identity governance and administration (IGA) and privileged access management (PAM) tools can ask machines the same questions asked of humans. An agent acting for a user should get at most that user's permissions, and each autonomous service needs its own identity, supervisor and role-specific permissions so its actions can be traced and its access revoked at machine speed. Citing Microsoft's deprecation of code access security and the early internet's turn to signatures and certificates, Garg writes that an agent's ability to reason about an action doesn't grant authority to take it, a decision that "must remain external to the model" and be enforced through identity infrastructure.


Sources:

  • Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Praerit Garg

item.title: AI Voice Agents Are Easy To Demo; Production Is Where The Engineering Begins
item.description:
Picolini, a technology executive whose company builds contact-center platforms, says voice AI demos are easy, but real calls bring degraded carrier audio, speakerphone background noise and brief acknowledgments, where a simple "okay" can stop an agent mid-explanation. Picolini recommends testing over actual phone routes, caching likely-needed customer data (some deployments use Redis) to avoid multi-second API waits, verifying identity rather than trusting a recognized number, and defining human-transfer triggers that pass along a concise summary. Some audio delays over SIP appeared only at thousands of concurrent calls, and as Picolini puts it, "A good demo proves the AI can talk."


Sources:

  • AI Voice Agents Are Easy To Demo; Production Is Where The Engineering Begins - forbes.com
item.dc:creator: Alexandro Picolini
